title: Two weeks ago I asked AI agents to build a modern-day grand strategy for me and my friends and here's where it is
author: rauf0300
selftext:
I’m a mobile developer, and I’d never made a game before. I like Hearts of Iron, and I wanted a present-day strategy game my friends and I could play over LAN in the same room, even on a weak laptop. Everyone picks a real country, runs its economy and politics, makes deals, and sooner or later someone argues about who owns the province next door. It runs in real time, with a pause button.

The agents wrote all the code while I made the decisions, played the builds and complained.

**What’s in the game after two weeks**

* 197 countries and 3,363 provinces. The game starts on 1 January 2026.
* You manage a budget and a construction queue, build power plants and develop transport corridors.
* There are parties, laws and elections. If you lose an election, you go into opposition and keep playing.
* The research tree has 250 nodes, and there are 96 weapon designs.
* NATO, the EU and CSTO are all in the game. Attack a NATO member and the whole bloc answers.
* You move your armies yourself. There are also air missions, fleets, blockades, intelligence, crises and ultimatums.
* Up to eight people can play on one network. A match takes anywhere from about 40 minutes to three hours.
* There are 17 tutorial lessons, in English and Russian.
* It’s built in Godot and C#, with about 250,000 lines of code and 1,189 automated tests.

**How I worked with the agents**

I started with Codex and the Superpowers plugin. I asked it to write a spec and ask me questions before it touched the code. The questions were better than I expected. “If you lose an election, is the game over?” I hadn’t thought about it when I was planing this game.

I kept switching tools as I hit limits. Gemini in Antigravity built the underlying rules and tests. DeepSeek in OpenCode drew the first map. Claude Code took over after that and has done everything since. The project keeps a record of what’s done and what’s next (Superpowers plugin), so each tool could pick up where the last one left off.

Claude Code hands tasks to sub-agents, checks what comes back and sends them back to fix things. They launch the game on my laptop, click through it and look at screenshots. I’d leave the laptop running overnight while I slept.

**Screenshots lie**

The game looked great in screenshots. Then I’d sit down to play and a button would work maybe one click in three. The game was rebuilding the order panel every in-game hour. At normal speed, that’s 24 times a second.

Then I sent French troops into Belgium. The preview said “this will start a war.” The troops walked into Brussels and stood there. Since France and Belgium are both in NATO, the rules engine treated it as an ally passing through. The map preview had its own copy of the rule and came up with a different answer. An agent found the mismatch after I asked it to play as a complete newcomer and tell me everything it didn’t understand.

Then a friend joined my game and couldn’t pick a country. On his screen, the side panel grew past the bottom of the window on the very first frame, taking the confirm button with it. At the same time, an invisible full-screen element was swallowing every click on the map. The search box was the only way to select a country.

After that, I asked for a more systematic check. The game now opens about 280 of its own screens in both languages, at two window sizes and two UI scales. It takes a screenshot of each one and measures every button. The first run flagged 871 places where something was covered or off-screen. Most of those came from one column of notification cards sitting on top of every window. Now the check runs after every round of changes.

I spent $5 on Gemini with the student plan, $20 on ChatGPT and $100 on Claude. This all ran on an 8 GB M1 MacBook. It ran out of disk space twice when macOS swap grew to 9 GB while the agents were running the game.

Everything you see in the video was captured in-engine. I’ve started the Steam process.
